segments.text: Picture 73.6 tons of armor, as heavy as 30 Ford F-150 pickup trucks, tearing across open desert at 40 miles per hour.
Inside, four soldiers get tossed around a cramped steel box.
Two and a half miles away, an enemy tank peeks over a ridge.
Three seconds later, it vanishes in a shower of molten sparks.
The Abrams never even touch the brakes.
From the outside, America's M1A2 Abrams looks like pure brute force, a massive slab of metal with a cannon on top.
Climb through the hatch, though, and almost nothing inside this $15 million machine works the way common sense says a tank should.
Its driver lies flat on his back with motorcycle handlebars.
Its gunner aims a mirror instead of a barrel.
Its shell casings burn into thin air.
And three dozen high-explosive rounds sit inches behind the crew's heads.
Yet, if they all blow up at once, everyone inside can still drive away alive.
Start with its most impossible trick.
Sniping a moving target over two miles away while flying across rough ground.
Bolt a cannon rigidly to a hull, and every bump sends your crosshairs jumping across the sky.
Yet holding five tons of gun steel frozen against rough terrain is a losing fight against inertia.
So, American engineers flip the problem upside down.
Instead of stabilizing the heavy cannon first, they stabilized a tiny mirror.
Inside the gunner's primary sight, dual-axis gyroscopes sense every pitch and roll thousands of times a second,
tilting that featherweight mirror in the opposite direction.
While 147,000 pounds of steel slams through ditches underneath,
the gunner's thermal view floats dead still, locked onto targets miles out through darkness, smoke, or blowing dust.
Behind and above the gunner sits the tank commander with his own 360-degree thermal periscope, the CITV.
Together, they run a lethal routine called Hunter Killer.
While the gunner lines up tank one, the commander already hunts tank two.
The instant the first shot fires, one button tap whips the gunner's sight straight onto the next threat.
Watch what happens in the blink before the gun roars.
Gripping dual handles tankers call the Cadillacs, the gunner bounces a laser off the enemy hull for exact yardage.
Instantly, the computer factors in crosswind, air pressure, ammo temperature, and track tilt.
It even checks a tiny mirror on the barrel tip, the muzzle reference sensor,
because hot desert sun beating on a steel tube expands the top metal enough to bend the barrel slightly downward.
Then, the gunner pulls the trigger.
And here comes the wildest secret.
If the tank just hit a crater and the barrel lags a hair behind that stabilized mirror, the gun refuses to fire.
The computer holds the pulse while electrohydraulic servos muscle the 120mm M256 smoothbore cannon into line.
The exact microsecond the barrel crosses the calculated path, a gate called coincidence firing,
the circuit closes and fires automatically.
Inside the turret, no giant brass casing ever clatters onto the floor.
Standard 120mm Abrams shells have walls molded from rigid propellant that burns up completely in the chamber,
dropping only an ashtray-sized metal base puck.
What screams out the muzzle depends on the target.
Against heavy armor, crews load the 56-pound M829A4, modern heir to the Gulf War's legendary silver bullet.
Hidden inside sits a finned dart no thicker than a broomstick, forged from depleted uranium, roughly 1.7 times denser than lead.
Leaving the barrel at over 5,400 feet per second, nearly Mach 5, over a mile every second, three lightweight sabot pedals peel away.
That solid dart carries zero explosives.
It kills by pure kinetic force.
While tungsten darts mushroom and blunt on impact, depleted uranium shears along microscopic crystal planes,
sharpening itself like a chisel as it carves through steel.
And because uranium dust is pyrophoric, the moment it pierces an enemy cabin,
superheated shavings ignite on contact with air into a 3,000-degree firestorm.
Against anything else, the ammo gets smart.
Crews once juggled four specialty rounds, including the M-1028 canister shell,
turning the cannon into a giant shotgun blasting 1,100 tungsten balls across 500 yards.
Today, metal rings on the base of the M-1147 advanced multipurpose round talk to breech pins milliseconds before launch,
programming one shell to explode on contact, delay through concrete bunker walls,
or airburst tungsten fragments over missile teams.
Back that up with 11,400 rounds for two 7.62mm M240 machine guns
and 900 rounds for a .50 caliber MA Deuce aimed from Under Armour via the Crow's remote station,
and nothing nearby survives.
Which raises a glaring mystery.
With all those computers and smart shells,
why is the fourth crewman still a 19-year-old soldier loading 56-pound rounds by hand
when Russian tanks switched to autoloaders 50 years ago?
Watch a Russian T-72 or T-90 take a hit, and you see why.
Its carousel autoloader stores two dozen shells right beneath the crew's boots.
One spark sets off the whole ring like a pressure cooker,
tossing a 15-ton turret 100 feet into the sky.
The Abrams follows the opposite rule.
Save the crew, even if the tank dies.
Of its 42 main rounds, 36 sit isolated at the rear of the turret bustle behind heavy sliding blast doors,
and crews often leave the six hull slots empty in combat.
Standing on the left side of the turret basket,
the loader bumps a pad with his leg, the famous knee switch,
snapping the hydraulic blast door open.
He rips out a shell, spins, drops his knee off the switch so the door slams shut in under two seconds,
rams the round home, and yells,
UP!
A sharp loader finishes that sprint in four seconds flat,
beating most autoloaders while giving the crew extra hands to fix tracks in the mud.
Suppose an enemy hit pierces that rear ammo bay and ignites 36 shells at once.
With the blast door shut, the explosion blows open thin roof panels above the rack,
venting a volcano of flame harmlessly skyward while four soldiers three feet away stay alive and keep rolling.
Punching through the front of an Abrams is even tougher.
Solid steel thick enough to stop modern missiles would push the tank past 120 tons.
Instead, its angled cheeks hide a classified Chobham-derived sandwich of ceramics,
elastic layers, heavy alloys, air gaps, and depleted uranium mesh,
shattering 25,000-foot-per-second shape-charge copper jets before they reach the cabin.
On the M1A2 SEP-V3, four flat Trophy radars guard 360 degrees around the turret.
When an RPG or missile streaks in,
side launchers whip around and blast metal pellets to shred the warhead mid-air.
And if a hit sparks an internal fuel flash,
optical sensors spot the flare in three milliseconds.
Flooding the bay with fire-suppressing gas in under 150 milliseconds,
before flames can blister skin.
Pentagon records prove what that means under fire.
A U.S. Government Accountability Office report on Operation Desert Storm
found that out of over 1,800 Abrams tanks deployed in 1991,
zero were destroyed by Iraqi fire,
and not one crewman died from an enemy tank shot.
When one M1A1 got stuck in deep mud,
crews dropped thermite inside and ordered another Abrams to shoot it with 120-millimeter rounds
to deny Iraq its classified armor.
Even after friendly shots cooked off its ammo,
the blowout panels vented the blast skyward and the hull refused to shatter.
So, how do you make 147,000-pound sprint without sinking into soft dirt?
Up in the nose, isolated from the spinning turret basket,
the driver reclines on his back beneath the gun,
steering with motorcycle-style T-bar handlebars.
Twist the grips back for throttle.
Push left or right,
and the Allison transmission spins the tracks at different speeds,
or opposite directions to pivot 73.6 tons in place.
Underneath, 14 dual road wheels twist steel torsion bars across the floor
like giant spring rods to swallow three-foot drops.
Wrapping them are 25-inch wide T-158 tracks that spread the load so wide,
the tank presses down at just 15.4 pounds per square inch,
less than half the air pressure in a family sedan's tires.
Under the rear deck sits a Honeywell AG T-1500 gas turbine,
essentially a modified helicopter jet engine.
Weighing 2,500 pounds, half a comparable tank diesel,
it cranks out 1,500 horsepower and 2,750 pound-feet of torque
with an eerie whine that earned the Abrams its Cold War nickname,
Whispering Death.
It normally drinks JP-8 jet fuel,
yet, in a pinch, burns diesel or gasoline,
while pulsejet air cleaners blast compressed air backward through the filters
to clear desert sand before it melts onto the turbine blades.
Yet, every superpower inside the M1A2 carries a brutal bill.
Out-the-tail grill pours 930-degree Fahrenheit exhaust,
hot enough to scorch friendly infantry behind the hull and glow on thermal sites.
Worse, fuel burn is measured in gallons per mile,
roughly 60 gallons an hour cross-country,
nearly 2 gallons per mile from its 505-gallon tanks,
and 10 gallons an hour just idling.
Engineers added an under-armor auxiliary power unit on the SEPV-3
so crews could run electronics on silent watch without draining fuel convoys.
Meanwhile, added armor pushed the SEPV-3 to 73.6 tons,
cracking rural bridges and straining recovery vehicles,
right as $500 kamikaze drones rewrote warfare.
Like all Cold War tanks, the Abrams stacked its uranium armor up front,
leaving the roof and engine deck thin.
As older M1A1s learned in Ukraine,
a cheap quadcopter diving onto the roof bypasses invincible frontal cheeks completely.
That collision of weight, fuel thirst, and top-attack drones
forced the U.S. Army to cancel the heavier SEPV-4
and fast-track a radical successor,
the M1E3 Abrams.
Entering early prototype testing by 2026,
it aims to shed nearly 14 tons towards 60 tons,
adopt a hybrid electric drive,
and seal three crewmen inside an armored hull capsule
beneath an unmanned, auto-loading turret
built to defeat drones from day one.
For four decades,
the M1A2 Abrams proved how far engineers could bend physics,
stabilizing tiny mirrors at 40 miles per hour,
taming ammo explosions with knee switches,
and strapping a jet turbine to 73 tons of uranium-laced steel.
Now, its survival depends on proving a heavyweight legend
can evolve faster than the threats hunting it from above.
